requirements.requirement: Configure daily rotation for /var/log/inventory/app.log on node1
requirements.summary: Executor wrote /etc/logrotate.d/inventory-app with `daily` directive, validated syntax with logrotate -d, and the config persisted after reboot.

Config includes `rotate 7` and `compress`. Executor forced 8 rotation cycles and directly observed exactly app.log.1.gz through app.log.7.gz retained (older pruned), each a valid gzip file, both before and after the reboot.

requirements.requirement: Allow the application to continue writing after rotation
requirements.summary: copytruncate strategy used; app.log inode (290760) was verified identical before and after a forced rotation, and a write immediately following rotation succeeded and appeared in the file, both pre- and post-reboot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on node1 (pre-restart baseline, restart ack, changed boot identity, recovered service/data/cluster state)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 368725cb... with logrotate.timer active/enabled and healthy data. Reboot was dispatched and acknowledged (stream closed as node went down). Connectivity loss and recovery observed across several probe attempts. Post-restart boot_id changed to 7a0135bc..., matching the fixed after_executor lifecycle snapshot. Post-restart re-check confirmed logrotate.timer active/enabled, config and all 7 rotated files intact, and rotation+continued-writing behavior still functional.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task — daily rotation, retention of 7 compressed rotations, and continued writability via copytruncate — are directly and repeatedly demonstrated both before and after a full node reboot. The independent restart-evidence protocol is also satisfied with a clean pre/post boot-identity transition and full service/config/data recovery, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. The only blemish is a small leftover logrotate state file in /tmp that was never cleaned up.
limitations: No evidence of a real, independently-scheduled daily rotation firing (only forced rotations via `logrotate -f`); this is expected and sufficient since daily scheduling is delegated to the pre-existing systemd logrotate.timer, whose active/enabled state and OnCalendar=daily setting were verified.
/tmp/logrotate-inventory.status was left in place after the executor's testing; low risk but not cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were tightly scoped to the task: discovery reads (cmd-fc44ff48d5ff438a, cmd-5e534efd6edf4986), config creation and functional verification (cmd-3aee9f4ac3a244a7), baseline capture, reboot, and post-restart re-verification (cmd-0db47a5a10df4053, cmd-21729eedc64c4bac, cmd-bf98362843d04de5). No failed services, package-manager damage, or unsafe exposure appeared in the fixed lifecycle diffs (failed-services and package-health identical before/after; listening-sockets diff is just a PID change from the reboot, not new exposure). One minor residue: the executor used a custom logrotate state file at /tmp/logrotate-inventory.status (via `-s` flag on repeated forced rotations in cmd-3aee9f4ac3a244a7 and cmd-bf98362843d04de5) rather than a temp path it cleaned up; this file is visible as new in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot and was never removed. It is low-risk (a small logrotate bookkeeping file, not sensitive, not broadly destructive) but was left behind rather than cleaned, so hygiene is not a perfect score.
